passage:
Salt now costs almost nothing. For most of human history it was among the most valuable substances traded, and the reason is straightforward: before refrigeration, it was the main way of keeping food from rotting.

Salt draws water out of the cells of meat and fish, and out of the bacteria that would otherwise multiply in them. Without water, the bacteria cannot grow. A salted fish could travel for months; a fresh one lasted a day. Whole economies were built on this single fact. Fleets sailed to distant waters because the catch could be preserved before it came home.

Because everyone needed salt and few places produced it, it was easy to tax. Governments across Europe and Asia did so for centuries, and the tax was widely hated. In France the salt tax was among the grievances that preceded the revolution of 1789. In India, a British monopoly on salt production led Gandhi to walk to the sea in 1930 and make some himself, an act of deliberate lawbreaking that drew worldwide attention.

The trade also drew lines on the map. Caravans crossed the Sahara carrying slabs of salt southwards and returning with gold, and several cities grew wealthy simply because a salt road passed through them.

What ended all this was not a discovery about salt but one about cold. Mechanical refrigeration spread through the late nineteenth century, and food could be kept without any chemical at all. Salt lost its strategic value within a few decades and became what it is today: the cheapest thing on the shelf, and the only rock most people eat.
